title: Exceptional Superconducting Interfaces between Graphene and Atomic Chains in A15-MoRe
authors: Hiroto Ogura, Yuto Tsukidate, Shun Kondo, Zhuoqun Li, Natsuki Sasaki, Tsunenobu Sato, Azusa Utsumi, Tomohiro Otsuka, Mitsuhiro Saito, Kazutoshi Inoue, Takashi Taniguchi, Kenji Watanabe, Yuichi Ikuhara, Toshiaki Kato
abstract: Realizing highly transparent and magnetic-field-resilient superconducting contacts is a critical bottleneck for the advancement of two-dimensional (2D) quantum devices. Molybdenum-rhenium (MoRe) alloys have been empirically favored as they uniquely yield ballistic, highly transparent contacts to graphene that survive in high-magnetic-field regimes; however, the microscopic origin of this anomalous transparency has remained a long-standing puzzle. Here, we resolve this paradox by revealing that pristine graphene/MoRe interfaces are governed by the classical A15 superconducting phase. Combining low-temperature transport, X-ray diffraction, and atomic-resolution electron microscopy, we demonstrate that as-deposited MoRe spontaneously forms the A15 phase in direct contact with graphene, whereas thermal annealing triggers a phase transition to a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure that severely degrades the Josephson transparency. Crucially, the one-dimensional (1D) transition-metal atomic chains unique to the A15 structure exhibit a near-perfect lattice match (mismatch < 1%) with graphene edges. First-principles calculations further prove that the d-orbitals of these historically renowned 1D chains possibly hybridize with graphene's Dirac cone near the K point. These findings not only uncover the structural and electronic origins of optimal MoRe contacts but also establish A15-phase superconductors as a geometrically ideal, universal platform for realizing robust quantum electronics based on 2D materials.
summary: This work investigates the superconducting interface between graphene and MoRe, finding that the exceptional performance relies on the metastable A15 crystal phase of MoRe. By combining transport, structural, and computational methods, the authors prove that the A15 phase provides both the necessary structural lattice match and the electronic coupling required for robust quantum devices.
main_problem: The study aims to resolve the microscopic origin of the anomalous, high transparency observed in superconducting contacts formed between graphene and Molybdenum-Rhenium (MoRe) alloys, particularly in high magnetic fields.
main_result: The optimal superconducting contact is achieved when the MoRe forms the metastable A15 superconducting phase in its as-deposited state, which exhibits near-perfect lattice matching with graphene edges and favorable electronic coupling.
method: The research combines low-temperature transport measurements, X-ray diffraction (XRD) to track phase transitions, atomic-resolution electron microscopy (STEM), and first-principles Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations.
model_or_system: The physical system is a Josephson junction (GJJ) formed by coupling graphene to MoRe electrodes. The key structural comparison is between the superconducting A15 phase and the insulating/degrading hexagonal close-packed (hcp) phase of MoRe.
key_observables: Zero-resistance state, critical current density, crystal phase identification (A15 vs. hcp), lattice mismatch ($	ext{mismatch} < 1\%$), and electronic orbital hybridization near the Dirac cone K point.
important_parameters: Annealing temperature (critical transition observed between $150^\circ	ext{C}$ and $900^\circ	ext{C}$), magnetic field strength, and lattice mismatch percentage.
main_assumptions: The high transparency is fundamentally linked to the structural commensurability and electronic coupling provided by the A15 phase.
figures_summary: Figures detail the degradation of zero-resistance states with annealing temperature (XRD/Transport), structural phase transitions ($	ext{A15} 	o 	ext{hcp}$), and DFT calculations confirming lattice matching and orbital hybridization.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of problem identification (anomalous transparency) $	o$ experimental characterization (transport/XRD/STEM showing phase dependence on annealing) $	o$ theoretical explanation (DFT confirming A15 structure's geometric and electronic suitability) $	o$ conclusion establishing A15 as the universal platform.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter superconductivity, the detailed study of interface engineering, structural phase stability, and electronic coupling mechanisms between 2D materials and superconductors is highly relevant to open quantum systems research.
